passages.title: The Personality of Long's Peak
passages.text:
Long's Peak, 14,700 feet high, blocks up one end of Estes Park, and dwarfs all the surrounding mountains. From it on this side rise, snow-born, the bright St. Vrain, and the Big and Little Thompson. By sunlight or moonlight its splintered grey crest is the one object which, in spite of wapiti and bighorn, skunk and grizzly, unfailingly arrests the eyes. From it come all storms of snow and wind, and the forked lightnings play round its head like a glory. It is one of the noblest of mountains, but in one's imagination it grows to be much more than a mountain. It becomes invested with a personality. In its caverns and abysses one comes to fancy that it generates and chains the strong winds, to let them loose in its fury. The thunder becomes its voice, and the lightnings do it homage. Other summits blush under the morning kiss of the sun, and turn pale the next moment; but it detains the first sunlight and holds it round its head for an hour at least, till it pleases to change from rosy red to deep blue; and the sunset, as if spell-bound, lingers latest on its crest. The soft winds which hardly rustle the pine needles down here are raging rudely up there round its motionless summit. The mark of fire is upon it; and though it has passed into a grim repose, it tells of fire and upheaval as truly, though not as eloquently, as the living volcanoes of Hawaii. Here under its shadow one learns how naturally nature worship, and the propitiation of the forces of nature, arose in minds which had no better light.

Long's Peak, "the American Matterhorn," as some call it, was ascended five years ago for the first time. I thought I should like to attempt it, but up to Monday, when Evans left for Denver, cold water was thrown upon the project. It was too late in the season, the winds were likely to be strong, etc.; but just before leaving, Evans said that the weather was looking more settled, and if I did not get farther than the timber line it would be worth going. Soon after he left, "Mountain Jim" came in, and said he would go up as guide, and the two youths who rode here with me from Longmount and I caught at the proposal. Mrs. Edwards at once baked bread for three days, steaks were cut from the steer which hangs up conveniently, and tea, sugar, and butter were benevolently added. Our picnic was not to be a luxurious or "well-found" one, for, in order to avoid the expense of a pack mule, we limited our luggage to what our saddle horses could carry. Behind my saddle I carried three pair of camping blankets and a quilt, which reached to my shoulders. My own boots were so much worn that it was painful to walk, even about the park, in them, so Evans had lent me a pair of his hunting boots, which hung to the horn of my saddle. The horses of the two young men were equally loaded, for we had to prepare for many degrees of frost.
passages.source_note: Public domain: from A Lady's Life in the Rocky Mountains by Isabella Bird (1879). Straight quotation marks substituted for typographic ones.

questions.stem: What can the reader tell about how the writer feels about Long's Peak overall?

options.text: She finds it dull compared with the lower hills
She admires it deeply, treating it almost as a living being
She is mainly frightened and wishes to leave it
She thinks it is smaller than travellers claim
She regrets that it hides the other peaks from view

questions.explanation: The mountain 'becomes invested with a personality' and is called 'one of the noblest of mountains', showing deep admiration rather than fear or indifference.

questions.stem: How does the writer's tone change when she turns from the mountain to the account of getting ready for the trip?

options.text: It becomes furious and bitter
It becomes frightened and panicked
It becomes mocking and sarcastic
It becomes plain and matter-of-fact, listing what was done
It stays exactly as grand and worshipful as before

questions.explanation: Once the writer moves on to Evans, Mountain Jim and the packing, she reports events plainly — bread baked, steaks cut, blankets carried — a matter-of-fact tone quite unlike the awe of the opening.

questions.stem: How high does the passage say Long's Peak is?

options.text: 7,500 feet
11,000 feet
1,500 feet
4,700 feet
14,700 feet

questions.explanation: The opening sentence states the peak is '14,700 feet high'.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which rivers rise from this side of the peak?

options.text: The Colorado and the Platte
The Snowy and the Denver
The St. Vrain and the Big and Little Thompson
The Longmount and the Matterhorn
The Estes and the Lily

questions.explanation: The text names 'the bright St. Vrain, and the Big and Little Thompson' as rising, snow-born, from this side.

questions.stem: The writer says the winds that 'hardly rustle the pine needles down here are raging rudely up there'. What is the main effect of this contrast?

options.text: It shows that the summit is a far wilder, harsher place than the sheltered valley below
It proves that no wind ever reaches the valley at all
It suggests the pine trees are dying from the cold
It tells the reader exactly how fast the wind is blowing
It shows the writer prefers the summit to the valley

questions.explanation: Setting the barely-stirring valley air against the winds 'raging rudely' at the top draws a sharp contrast that makes the summit feel a much wilder and more dangerous world than the calm valley.

questions.stem: In the phrase that the crest 'unfailingly arrests the eyes', what does 'arrests' mean here?

options.text: Places under guard
Catches and holds
Tires and blinds
Frees and releases
Injures and hurts

questions.explanation: To 'arrest' the eyes means to catch and hold the gaze, not to stop a criminal; the crest always seizes the viewer's attention.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention 'wapiti and bighorn, skunk and grizzly' when describing the crest?

options.text: To warn readers that the animals are dangerous to hunt
To explain what the travellers ate on the journey
To prove the region has no interesting scenery
To show the animals live only on the summit
To stress that even striking wildlife cannot draw the eyes away from the crest

questions.explanation: By listing striking wild animals that might otherwise seize a traveller's notice, she stresses that even they cannot pull the eyes away from the crest, which 'unfailingly' dominates.

questions.stem: What does the second paragraph mainly do in the passage?

options.text: To describe the shape and colours of the crest
To explain how the rivers are formed by the snow
To tell how the climb was proposed and how the party got ready
To argue that mountain worship is foolish
To warn the reader about dangerous wild animals

questions.explanation: The second paragraph turns from portraying the peak to the story of the trip — Evans's doubts, Mountain Jim offering to guide, and the food and blankets being made ready — so its job is to narrate the plan and preparations.

questions.stem: Why does Mrs. Edwards bake bread and cut steaks before the group sets off?

options.text: Because the shops in Denver had all closed
Because the group will be away camping for several days
Because the horses refused to move without food
Because a storm was expected to trap them at the cabin
Because Mountain Jim demanded a farewell feast

questions.explanation: The party is preparing food to carry because they will be away camping 'for three days', so provisions must be made ready in advance.

questions.stem: When the writer says 'cold water was thrown upon the project', she means that people

options.text: poured water over the camping supplies
washed the horses before the long ride
discouraged the plan and raised objections to it
welcomed the plan with great excitement
delayed the trip because of heavy rain

questions.explanation: To throw cold water on a plan is to discourage it; others raised objections such as the lateness of the season and the strong winds.

questions.stem: Which detail from the passage best supports the idea that the writer treats the peak as if it were alive?

options.text: 'was ascended five years ago for the first time'
'we limited our luggage to what our saddle horses could carry'
'the winds were likely to be strong'
'steaks were cut from the steer'
'The thunder becomes its voice, and the lightnings do it homage'

questions.explanation: The clearest evidence is that 'The thunder becomes its voice, and the lightnings do it homage', which gives the mountain a voice and subjects, exactly as a living ruler would have.

questions.stem: Who offered to go up the peak as the group's guide?

options.text: Griffith Evans
Mrs. Edwards
Mountain Jim
A youth from Denver
St. Vrain

questions.explanation: The passage states that 'Mountain Jim came in, and said he would go up as guide'.

questions.stem: In 'Other summits blush under the morning kiss of the sun', which device is the writer using?

options.text: Personification
Onomatopoeia
Simile
Alliteration
Rhyme

questions.explanation: Summits cannot really 'blush' or receive a 'kiss'; these are human actions given to the hills and the sun, so it is personification.

questions.stem: In 'though it has passed into a grim repose', what word class is 'repose'?

options.text: Verb
Noun
Adjective
Adverb
Preposition

questions.explanation: Here 'repose' names a state of rest and follows 'a grim', so it is being used as a noun.

questions.stem: The writer explains that the season was already too late and that strong winds were likely before the party had even set out. Including this mainly serves to:

options.text: To persuade the reader never to climb any mountain
To prove that Evans wanted the money for himself
To explain why the rivers were frozen over
To fill space until the horses were ready
To show that the attempt was risky and far from certain to succeed

questions.explanation: By setting out the reasons against going — the lateness of the season and the strong winds — before she agrees to try, the writer makes clear the climb was a risky undertaking with no guarantee of success.

questions.stem: The writer calls the peak 'one of the noblest of mountains'. Which word keeps the admiring shade of meaning of 'noblest'?

options.text: Tallest
Oldest
Coldest
Nearest
Most magnificent

questions.explanation: 'Noblest' praises the mountain as grand and worthy of respect; 'most magnificent' keeps that admiring, dignified sense, while 'tallest' or 'oldest' are merely factual.

questions.stem: What does the preparation of food tell us about the people at the cabin?

options.text: They were generous and helpful towards the travellers
They were secretive and unwilling to share
They were careless and forgot to pack supplies
They disliked the writer and hoped she would fail
They were wealthy townsfolk unused to the country

questions.explanation: Bread baked 'for three days' and butter 'benevolently added' show the cabin folk were generous and helpful in equipping the party for the trip.

questions.stem: How long ago does the passage say the peak was first climbed?

options.text: Five years ago
Fifty years ago
Three years ago
Ten years ago
The previous winter

questions.explanation: The text says it 'was ascended five years ago for the first time'.

questions.stem: Why did the travellers keep their luggage light?

options.text: Because the cabin had no spare bags to lend
Because the trail was flooded and slippery
Because they planned to be gone only one hour
To avoid the extra cost of hiring a pack mule
Because Mountain Jim ordered them to travel light

questions.explanation: They 'limited our luggage to what our saddle horses could carry' in order to 'avoid the expense of a pack mule', so cost drove the choice.

questions.stem: Evans said 'the weather was looking more settled'. What does 'settled' mean here?

options.text: Paid for in full
Sinking downwards
Newly arrived
Calm and steady
Argued over

questions.explanation: Applied to weather, 'settled' means calm and steady, likely to stay fair, which is why the climb suddenly seemed worth attempting.

questions.stem: Which of these is an example of a simile in the passage?

options.text: 'it becomes invested with a personality'
'the mark of fire is upon it'
'the forked lightnings play round its head like a glory'
'its motionless summit'
'the forces of nature'

questions.explanation: A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; 'the forked lightnings play round its head like a glory' is the comparison that uses 'like'.

questions.stem: In 'its splintered grey crest', which word is an adjective describing 'crest'?

options.text: Splintered
Crest
Its
Rise
Come

questions.explanation: 'Splintered' and 'grey' both describe the crest; of the options, 'splintered' is the adjective, while 'crest' is a noun and 'round' a preposition elsewhere.

questions.stem: How is the whole passage shaped?

options.text: From the summit downwards to the valley floor
From the present day back to the writer's childhood
From a list of dangers to a list of rewards
From a portrait of the mountain to the practical plans and packing beforehand
From one climber's view to another climber's view

questions.explanation: It moves from a vivid portrait of the mountain's grandeur to the practical account of deciding to climb and packing for it, so it goes from description to preparation.

questions.stem: Why does the writer mention that they 'had to prepare for many degrees of frost'?

options.text: To explain that the horses had never been ridden before
To prove the group had far too much luggage
To suggest the trip would only last a single afternoon
To show the reader how bitterly cold the higher ground was expected to be
To show the writer disliked the other travellers

questions.explanation: Preparing 'for many degrees of frost' tells the reader they expected severe cold on the higher ground, which is why the horses were loaded with blankets and warm gear.

questions.stem: When the writer says she and the youths 'caught at the proposal', she means they

options.text: threw the plan away in disgust
seized the offer eagerly and agreed at once
failed to understand what was suggested
grabbed hold of Mountain Jim's coat
argued about the plan for a long time

questions.explanation: To 'catch at' an offer is to seize it eagerly; the group jumped at Mountain Jim's suggestion to guide them up the peak.
